The maqam is a melodic system fundamental to Arabic classical music, analogous to the Indian raga. Each maqam is a framework of notes, characteristic phrases, and emotional associations within which musicians improvise and perform composed pieces. With its microtonal intervals—quarter-tones unavailable in Western notation—ornamented phrasing, and emotional intensity, maqam music expresses the aesthetic values of the Arab world across the Levant, Egypt, Iraq, and the Gulf.

The maqam system includes numerous named modes, with over seventy major maqams existing alongside hundreds of variants. Each is associated with emotional states and seasons or times of day. Intervals smaller than the Western semitone—quarter-tones—are central to the tradition. The same note can be played flat or natural, creating a tonal palette foreign to Western equal temperament. The oud, a lute, and the qanun, a zither, are the primary maqam instruments. The human voice is equally valued, and singers must master the microtonal inflections and ornamentation integral to the tradition.

Performances typically begin with a free-rhythm improvisation called the taqsim, progress to a slower composed piece, and culminate in rapid rhythmic sections. The structure mirrors the Hindustani alap-jor-jhala progression. The maqam tradition was significantly documented and standardized during the Ottoman Empire. The Baghdad School of the nineteenth century produced notable systematizations and famous composers like Mulla Othman. Urban court music, folk traditions, and religious music all employ the maqam system, making it a unifying musical language across social contexts. Modern maqam players like Oum Kulthum became icons of Arab culture. The tradition remains vital in contemporary Arab music and cinema.
